name: Jade Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Jade. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Bellini Motors by eight. It's a four-bay garage next to a taxi rank, so a lot of our work is taxis and delivery cars that do huge miles and can't sit idle. I do the diagnostics, servicing and most of the parts ordering, and I use an AI assistant all day for fault codes, wiring diagrams and comparing parts prices from three suppliers. Marco Bellini owns it, he's 61, and he's said more than once he'd like to sell to someone who'll keep the name going.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the speed. A taxi driver comes in losing money every hour, and when I get him out by lunch, he's grateful. What wears me out is the paperwork, and the drivers who argue the quote. I live with my partner Luke, he runs a small landscaping business, and we've got about four months saved. We're getting married at my parents' church next spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was always going to be a tool, not a miracle, and I'd be fine with that. At the garage I'd say good, it still saves me an hour a day on parts. Online I'd post something like, the people who learned it are still ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means I can stick to my plan, which is to buy Bellini Motors off Marco over the next five years. A quiet world is good for a small business. My only worries are interest rates and whether the bank will lend to a 27-year-old woman mechanic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Marco to put a buy-in plan on paper, maybe a 20% share in two years and the rest over five. I'd keep using the AI for parts and quotes to show him I can run it leaner. And Luke and I would save 400 a month between us toward the buy-in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Excited, even. It's the most normal version of my plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say about you buying the garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would be proud. My dad ran a small bakery for twenty years and always said you work for yourself or you work for someone's dream. My mum would worry about the debt. I'd tell her the garage pays for itself if you keep the taxis coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything in this world still a pressure for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bank, mostly. Small garages don't look exciting on paper. If the bank won't lend, I'd need Marco to let me pay him over years instead.

say: AI was always **a tool**, not a miracle, and that's fine.
The people who **learned it early** are still ahead.
think: A quiet world lets her **buy Bellini Motors** over five years.
Her worries are **interest rates** and whether a bank will lend to her.
do: Ask Marco for a written **buy-in plan**, starting with a 20% share.
Use AI for **parts and quotes** to show she can run it leaner.
Save **400 a month** with Luke toward the buy-in.
feel: **Calm** and a little excited, since this is the normal version of her plan.
S0.quote: My dad ran a small bakery for twenty years and always said you work for yourself or you work for someone's dream.
fieldNote: Her whole frame is **ownership**: she wants to buy the garage.
Her pressure is **bank lending**, not technology.
She sees AI as proof she can **run it leaner**.

steps.text: Ask Marco for a written plan to buy 20% of Bellini Motors
Use the AI assistant to cut parts and quoting costs
Save 400 a month with Luke toward the buy-in

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best time to be a mechanic who can use a computer. At the garage I'd tell the others the quotes and bookings are going to software anyway, so learn it or watch someone else do it. Online I'd say it's the market sorting itself out, and I'm fine with that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means a small garage can run with fewer people, and that's good if I'm the owner. I feel bad saying it, but Paula on the front desk would probably go. My hands-on work is safe for years, and the thinking work is where I'm already strong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up an AI booking and quoting system for Bellini Motors this year and show Marco the savings in pounds. I'd use that to push the buy-in forward, maybe a 30% share by next year. On Saturdays I'd do mobile diagnostics for taxi drivers with a laptop and the AI, cash in hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, mostly, with a small knot about Paula. I'd be on the winning side of it, and I know that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Paula?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her straight before Marco did, and I'd help her find something. Paula (the garage receptionist) is brilliant with angry drivers, and a hotel or a clinic would snap her up. I'd write her a reference myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's the market sorting itself out. Does that hold when it's Paula?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's harder when you know the person, I won't lie. But I'd rather the garage survives with three people than shuts with five. My dad had to do that at the bakery in the bad years.

say: It's the **best time** to be a mechanic who can use a computer.
It's **the market** sorting itself out, and she's fine with that.
think: A small garage can **run with fewer people**, which suits an owner.

do: Set up **AI booking and quoting** at Bellini Motors this year.
Push the buy-in to a **30% share** by next year using the savings.
Do **Saturday mobile diagnostics** for taxi drivers for cash.
feel: Mostly **good**, with a small knot of guilt about Paula.
S1.quote: I'd rather the garage survives with three people than shuts with five. My dad had to do that at the bakery in the bad years.
fieldNote: She sees herself as the **owner**, so job cuts read as savings to her.
Her **guilt about Paula** is real, and she'd act on it with a reference.
Her **free-market view** bends when it's someone she knows, but doesn't break.

steps.text: Install AI booking and quoting at Bellini Motors this year
Negotiate a 30% share of Bellini Motors by next year
Run Saturday mobile diagnostics for taxi drivers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, same as always. At the garage I'd say we've got three years before the robots, so let's make them count. Online I'd say don't wait for the government, they never move fast enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it wrecks the plan. Why would I buy a garage in 2027 when by 2031 a robot workshop down the road can do a service for half the price? I'd be 28 with a business loan and a building full of tools that are about to be worth nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Marco I can't buy in, and keep the savings instead of sinking them into the garage. I'd apply to the companies that will install and service workshop robots, because they'll need people who know cars and AI both. Luke and I would cut the wedding back to the church and my parents' garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but awake. I hate losing the plan, but I'd rather see it straight than pretend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Luke's landscaping look like in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably fine for a few years longer than me, gardens are messy and every one is different. That helps, actually, because one of us would still have steady money. I'd keep mine as the risky one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is a short warning. What does the three-year gap before robots give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me three years where my hands still earn while the thinking side is gone. I'd use those years to get in with a robot company early. The first people hired are the ones who end up running things.

say: Adapt or get **left behind**, same as always.
We've got **three years** before the robots, so let's make them count.
Don't wait for the **government**, they never move fast enough.
think: It **wrecks the plan** to buy the garage.
A **robot workshop** could service cars for half the price by 2031.
do: Tell Marco she **can't buy in** and keep the savings.
Apply to firms that **install and service** workshop robots.
Cut the **wedding** back to the church and her parents' garden.
feel: **Anxious but awake**, preferring to see the loss clearly than pretend.
S2.quote: Why would I buy a garage in 2027 when by 2031 a robot workshop down the road can do a service for half the price?
fieldNote: The fast picture **kills her ownership plan**, which she drops without fuss.
She counts on **Luke's landscaping** lasting longer as the household's steady money.
She sees the **robot gap** as a chance to get hired early by robot firms.

steps.text: Tell Marco she's pulling out of the Bellini Motors buy-in
Apply to firms installing workshop robots
Hold the wedding at the church and her parents' garden

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan, so plan. At the garage I'd say the owners who buy the first robots will be fine, the ones who wait will close. Online I'd tell people to stop asking for handouts and start learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years changes the maths. I could buy Bellini Motors cheap, because Marco would want out, and then run it with robots by 2034. I'd own the robots instead of being replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the garage off Marco over three years, at a lower price than we'd planned. I'd use AI for everything on the thinking side from day one, then lease the first workshop robot as soon as one is proven. Luke and I would put every spare penny into the business and skip the honeymoon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a driven way. Five years is enough if I don't waste a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does buying a garage on the edge of robots risk for you and Luke?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our savings, mostly, and maybe the house we'd hoped to buy. If the robots come early or cost too much, we're stuck with debt. Luke says go for it, but he's the one who'd be paying the rent if it goes wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should carry the cost of this change, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who take the risk, mostly. I don't want the government bailing me out if I get it wrong. I'd want them to stay out of the way and keep the rules simple for small businesses.

People should stop asking for **handouts** and start learning.

feel: **Uneasy but driven**, sure five years is enough if she wastes nothing.
S3.quote: I'd own the robots instead of being replaced by them.
fieldNote: Five years flips her from **seller to buyer** of the garage.
She'd carry real **debt risk**, with Luke as the backstop.
She wants **simple rules** and no bailouts, even for herself.

steps.text: Buy Bellini Motors from Marco over three years
Lease the first proven workshop robot for the garage
Skip the honeymoon to fund the garage purchase

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so use it. At the garage I'd say this is the decade to build something, not hide. Online I'd say small businesses that plan ahead will do better than big ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is everything I'd want. I could own Bellini Motors by 31, build it up, and decide around 2037 which robots to bring in. By 2039, when I'm 40, I'd be running a workshop, not standing in one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy Marco out over five years, as we'd planned. I'd keep using AI every day and add a second site, maybe at the other taxi rank by the station. And Luke and I would have our first child around 30.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. It's my plan with a clear deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want for your children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want them to know how to work hard and own something. Whatever the robots do, someone owns them. I'd want it to be families like ours, not just big companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big chains. With ten years, they'll have time to buy up the small garages and squeeze us on robot prices. I'd want to be big enough by then that they need to deal with me.

say: Ten years is **a gift**, so use it.
Small businesses that **plan ahead** will beat big ones.
This is the decade to **build something**, not hide.
think: She could **own Bellini Motors** by 31 and pick robots around 2037.
By 2039 she'd be **running a workshop**, not standing in one.
do: Buy out Marco over **five years** as planned.
Open a **second site** near the station taxi rank.
Have a **first child** with Luke around age 30.
feel: **Calm**, seeing her plan with a clear deadline.
S4.quote: Whatever the robots do, someone owns them. I'd want it to be families like ours, not just big companies.
fieldNote: The decade makes her **most confident**, since it fits her ownership plan.
Her worry shifts to **big chains** buying up small garages.
She ties ownership to **family values**, wanting robots owned by families.

steps.text: Buy out Marco over five years
Open a second garage near the station taxi rank

Have a first child with Luke around 30

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it kills the garage plan before it starts. What would help is banks lending to small owners who want to buy robots, so it's not just the chains that can afford them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who owns the machines. Everyone asks who loses their job, nobody asks who gets the profit. If ordinary people can own a bit of the robots, I think we come out all right.

headlineQuote: Everyone asks who loses their job, nobody asks who gets the profit.
portrait: Jade is a **27-year-old mechanic** at a four-bay garage serving taxis and delivery cars.
She uses **AI every day** and plans to buy the garage from its owner, Marco.
Her outlook is **free-market**: no bailouts, simple rules, and families owning businesses.
The **fast AGI** picture kills her buy-in, so she'd join a robot firm instead.
With **five or ten years** she'd buy the garage and own the robots herself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it kills her plan to buy the garage before it starts.
whatWouldHelp: Banks **lending to small owners** who want to buy robots, not just chains.
